title: Forensics and Incident Response
objective: By the end of this lesson you can run the incident-response phases in order, preserve evidence by order of volatility and chain of custody, and choose containment, eradication, and recovery actions that fit the scenario.

rows: Playbooks, tools, contacts, training, before anything happens
An alert becomes a confirmed incident; scope and severity are set
Stop the spread: isolate hosts, block addresses, disable accounts
Remove the cause: malware, accounts, backdoors, the exploited flaw
Restore from clean sources, validate, return to service
Post-incident review; fix the gaps the incident exposed

blocks.text: Containment has a short-term and a long-term face: isolate the machine now, then decide whether to keep it isolated, rebuild it, or watch it as part of deeper investigation. Eradication without fixing the entry point guarantees a return visit, which is why the exploited vulnerability belongs in the eradication list.

Evidence disappears fastest where it is most fleeting. Collect from most to least volatile: CPU registers and cache, then RAM including running processes and network connections, then temporary files, then disk, then logs and archived data. RAM is the classic exam answer: pull it first, because shutting down destroys it.

items: Chain of custody: a record of who held the evidence, when, and what was done to it; unbroken, or the evidence loses standing.
Legal hold: preserve everything related to the case once litigation or investigation is expected.
Hash evidence at acquisition: prove the copy matches the original.
Work on copies, with write blockers for original media.
Documentation timestamps in a defensible timeline.

blocks.title: First responder rule
blocks.text: The most common exam mistake is a helpful technician reimaging the machine before evidence is captured. Isolate, preserve, capture volatile data, then clean. Rebuilding first destroys the answers.

blocks.title: Triage one alert
steps: Scenario: EDR flags a workstation beaconing to an unknown host at night; the user reports nothing.
Write your first three actions in order, naming the IR phase for each.
List what you would capture before any cleanup, in volatility order.
Write the one question the lessons-learned meeting must answer.
blocks.expected: Contain: isolate the host from the network (containment). Detect and analyze: pull EDR telemetry and authentication logs to set scope (detection and analysis). Preserve: RAM and connection data first, then disk and logs. Lessons learned must answer how the initial access happened and which control would have caught it sooner.

blocks.title: Lab: Windows Event Log Triage
blocks.description: Find failed logons (event 4625) and new account creation (event 4720) in your own Windows VM, or failed SSH logons in Linux auth.log, then write a three-line triage note. Full guide: labs/windows-event-log-triage.en.md.

blocks.title: Lab: Volatility Order
blocks.description: Drag the five evidence classes into the order a first responder collects them, most fleeting first, and defend why RAM comes before disk. Full design: labs/volatility-order.lab.en.md.

cheatsheet: IR phases: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.
Order of volatility: registers and cache, RAM, temp files, disk, logs and archives. Capture RAM before shutdown.
Chain of custody: unbroken record of handling; hash at acquisition; work on copies with write blockers.
Contain first, eradicate the cause (including the exploited flaw), then restore from clean sources.
Never reimage before volatile evidence is captured.

checkpoint.prompt: An analyst arrives at a compromised, still-running laptop. Which evidence should be captured first?

choices.A: The contents of RAM, including running processes and connections

checkpoint.explanation: RAM vanishes at shutdown, so it sits highest in the order of volatility for a live machine. Disk, archives, and rule lists all survive longer.

checkpoint.prompt: After an incident, the team removes the malware but leaves the unpatched web flaw it used. Which phase was left incomplete?
checkpoint.explanation: Eradication removes the cause, including the exploited vulnerability, so the same door closes. Recovery restores service; it cannot substitute for closing the entry point.
